title: Today, Solve a Problem
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart recalls his engineer father's maxim that there are only problem-makers and problem-solvers, and applies it to teacher identity and burnout. He argues that the apparent third category, the person who merely points out problems, collapses into problem-making, because copy-room complaining feels like camaraderie but leaves everyone more discouraged and feeds the burnout that sets in by May. His remedy is internal and small: build a problem-solver identity through daily, tiny acts of solving problems, such as unjamming a locker or a copier. To make the habit stick he borrows BJ Fogg's idea that you must celebrate each small success, because emotion is what creates habits. The piece frames this as a way to reclaim agency in a national conversation that often ignores teacher voice.
points: Complaining conversations feel good in the moment but compound into discouragement, which Stuart links to end-of-year burnout.
Agency does not require new authority; it requires a stubborn internal shift toward a problem-solver stance.
Identity is built by repeated small problem-solving, starting at the level of a jammed locker and working up to thornier issues.
Borrowing BJ Fogg, Stuart insists the celebration step is mandatory because positive emotion right after a behavior is what cements the habit.
quotes: Dave, there are two kinds of people in this world: problem-makers and problem-solvers. No one sits on the sidelines. Be a problem-solver, and you’ll succeed.

But when the conversation ends with only a mildly relieved sense that we found someone to commiserate with, it ends in the problem-making category. Everyone involved in the complaining conversation we’ve just had now possesses a new dose of that most nefarious form of discouragement — the one that feels good on top (because, after all, in finding a willing partner to complain with, we’ve found camaraderie) yet leaves us a bit more listless, powerless, devoid of life below the surface.

Positioning ourselves as problem-solvers gives us agency in a national conversation about education that seems, too often, bent on removing teacher voice and teacher empowerment. Luckily, problem-solving today doesn’t depend on someone walking up and granting us newfound authority; we need a simple, stubborn internal shift far more than a grandiose change in authority.

To make problem-solving a part of our identity, we need to regularly solve problems. If we’re to regularly solve problems, we need to habituate problem-solving. To habituate problem-solving, we need to celebrate each time we solve a problem.

If you want to create a habit, the celebration is not optional. The positive emotion you feel right after doing the behavior is what helps you remember to do the behavior again in the future. My headline: Emotions create habits.

This internal work isn’t optional if you’re going to enjoy a career in education, a career bent on solving problems millions of times bigger than you. Like my dad says, there are two kinds of people in this world.
